title: Houthis Strike Riyadh Amid Trump’s U.S. Role Debate in Expanding Mideast Conflict
body:
Saudi Arabia’s capital was rocked by a fresh missile and drone barrage from Yemen’s Iran‑backed Houthi rebels on Tuesday, a development that coincided with former President Donald Trump’s public musings about a possible U.S. response to the widening Middle‑East conflict. The attacks, which the Houthis said were “retaliation” for Saudi involvement in the war in Gaza, caused brief disruptions at King Khalid International Airport and prompted the kingdom to temporarily suspend flights before resuming operations. Despite the escalation, Saudi officials confirmed that the country will go ahead with the high‑profile Global Investment Forum in Riyadh next week, offering both on‑site and virtual participation and arranging alternative air and land routes for attendees.

The Houthi offensive marks a notable shift in the regional theatre. Since the outbreak of the Israel‑Hamas war in October, the rebels have stepped up their long‑standing campaign against Saudi interests, launching dozens of long‑range missiles and unmanned aerial systems that have struck oil facilities, commercial ships in the Red Sea and now, for the first time, the Saudi capital itself. In a televised statement, Houthi commander Abdul‑Maqsood al‑Houthi declared that the strikes were “a warning to those who support the aggression against Gaza,” and vowed that “more attacks will follow until justice is served.” Analysts say the move is designed to pressure Riyadh, which has been a vocal supporter of Israel and a key conduit for U.S. and Western aid to the Gaza front.

Washington’s reaction remains tentative. While President Joe Biden’s administration has condemned the Houthi attacks and pledged to bolster Saudi air defenses, the former president’s recent comments—suggesting that the United States might consider “a stronger hand” in the new front—have stirred speculation about a potential shift in policy. Trump, speaking at a rally in Florida, hinted that the U.S. could reassess its “limited engagement” strategy and consider direct action to protect allies and secure maritime routes. Diplomatic circles caution that any escalation could risk drawing the United States deeper into a conflict that already involves multiple state and non‑state actors, including Iran, which continues to supply the Houthis with weapons and technology.

The economic implications of the attacks are already being felt. The Global Investment Forum, slated to attract more than 30,000 investors, CEOs and policymakers, is a cornerstone of Saudi Vision 2030, aimed at diversifying the kingdom’s oil‑dependent economy. Organizers have reassured participants that security measures have been heightened and that virtual attendance options will allow uninterrupted engagement. Nevertheless, some multinational firms have expressed concerns over supply‑chain disruptions in the Red Sea, where Houthi strikes have already caused a surge in shipping insurance premiums and prompted several major carriers to reroute vessels around the Cape of Good Hope.

Regional experts underscore that the Houthis’ new focus on Riyadh could signal a broader strategy to force Saudi Arabia to recalibrate its stance on the Gaza war. “By targeting the heart of the kingdom, the Houthis are attempting to make the conflict less abstract for Saudi leaders and citizens,” said Dr. Leila Al‑Saadi, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. “If Riyadh perceives a direct threat to its core infrastructure, it may pressure Washington to adopt a more assertive posture, which could further destabilize an already volatile region.”

Looking ahead, the convergence of Houthi aggression, U.S. political rhetoric and Saudi economic ambitions creates a precarious balance. The upcoming investment summit will serve as a litmus test for the kingdom’s resilience and its ability to shield critical projects from security shocks. Meanwhile, the international community watches closely to see whether Washington will translate Trump’s provocative language into concrete policy or maintain its current diplomatic approach. The next weeks are likely to define whether the Middle East’s newest front will remain a series of isolated strikes or evolve into a sustained campaign that reshapes regional alliances and global energy markets.
